beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Kavya, and this video is about catching AI-generated junk before it hits your data pipeline. Quick note: the voice you're hearing is AI, Kokoro text-to-speech reading a script I drafted with help from Claude Code. In my demo batch of rider feedback, half the rows are junk. Load it all, and the average rating looks great. So what should stand between that batch and your dashboard?

props.command: Half of a rider-feedback batch is junk: copied comments, impossible values, rows with no source. Loaded straight in, the average rating looks great. What should check a batch before it reaches my pipeline?
props.runningText: loading the same batch with and without a gate…
output: no gate: 20 rows loaded, average rating 4.30
true average 3.40; 1 junk row still passed

beats.narration_text: Here's the idea: you can't reliably spot AI-written text by its style, so don't try. Check the data itself: where each row came from, whether its values can exist, and whether it's a copy, before it lands.

props.text:
Catching AI junk means spotting AI text.
Source, ranges, copies: then load.

beats.narration_text: Strip a validation gate down and it's four checks. Provenance: every row says where it came from. Ranges: a rating of seven, or a zero-minute trip with a ninety-five dollar fare, can't exist. Near-duplicates: the same comment, reworded again and again. And quarantine, not delete, so a person can review what was held back. None of it guesses who wrote the text.

beats.narration_text: So I ran it. Twenty rider-feedback rows, synthetic, and half of them are junk. Loaded with no checks, all twenty go in. The average rating comes out at four point three, and eleven of twenty rows are five stars. On a dashboard, that reads like riders love the service. It's mostly the junk talking.

shot.visual_intent: Real terminal run of demo/junk_gate_demo.py ungated; verbatim stdout, each line timed to the narration; the average-rating line carries the one highlight.

out.text: gate checks data properties, not writing style

beats.narration_text: Same batch, through the gate. Nine rows are quarantined: three with no source, four with impossible values, two near-copies. The average drops to three point five five. The true average, real rows only, is three point four. One junk row still got through: the first copy of the template, because its twin was rejected for a different reason first. And nothing is deleted.

beats.narration_text: To be fair, this gate checks the data, not the writing. A fake row with a real-looking source, possible values and fresh wording would pass. One already did here: the first copy of the template. And my data is synthetic, built so half is junk, so this shows the method, not a real junk rate. What it does catch: unknown origins, impossible values, and copies.

beats.narration_text: Recap. A validation gate is provenance, range checks, a near-duplicate check, and quarantine. With no gate, junk pushed the average rating to four point three. With the gate, nine rows were held back and the average fell to three point five five, close to the true three point four. The boundary: fluent, plausible fakes still pass. So gate every batch, and still sample some rows by hand.

artifactLines: Validation gate = provenance + range checks + near-duplicate check + quarantine.
No gate: 20 rows loaded, average rating 4.30, 11 of 20 five-star.
Gate: 9 quarantined, average 3.55; true average 3.40; 1 junk row passed.
Boundary: it checks the data, not the prose; fluent fakes get through.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Ask Claude exactly this: look at one batch my pipeline ingested this week. Which rows have no source, impossible values, or near-duplicate text? Draft the checks that should quarantine them before they load. Watch which rule catches the most rows. That's where your junk is coming from.
